name: Ben Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pretty ordinary, which I'm a bit proud of. I'm doing computer science with a lot of maths in it, and I rent a room in a shared house with three other students, about twenty minutes by bike from campus. Mornings are lectures, afternoons are either labs or the library, and I work Wednesday evenings and all day Sunday at a bike repair shop. The owner, a man called Gus, pays cash and lets me fix whatever's in the back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Why the bike shop and not something on campus?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It was the first place that said yes, and I liked it from the first day. I can fix a gear problem in ten minutes and a customer leaves happy, which doesn't happen with code assignments. It also pays a bit better than the campus cafe, which was offering me six hours a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, told you so, and then I'd feel a bit guilty for saying it. I'd tell my housemates it's a decent tool, like a calculator, and then people will stop arguing about it. At the bike shop we've got a stock app that sort of does what Gus's notebook did, and the notebook is still on the shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel like things carry on, which is fine but not great. My loan covers fees, my wages cover food and rent, and there's no spare. If the bike shop had a slow winter and cut my hours, I'd be in trouble, and that has nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, and I'd use an AI assistant a bit more for explaining maths, since it's handy and I already use it now and then. I'd ask Gus for an extra weekday shift in the busy season. And I'd start a small emergency fund, even if it takes a year to get to a few hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Slightly flat, to be honest. A normal world is where nobody's surprised and I keep an eye on my bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in your bank balance in a normal winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gets low in January, because the shop is quiet and my rent is the same. In a normal winter I cut my shifts by a third and start eating the same pasta every night, so my worry isn't about robots. I just want a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the assistant now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For explaining proofs in a different way and for checking my code for silly mistakes. I don't copy answers, because the exam doesn't let me. It's like a patient friend who sometimes talks nonsense.

say: I'd say it's a decent **tool**, like a calculator.
I'd tell housemates at the bike shop the stock app didn't remove the **notebook**.
think: Things carry on, which is fine, but I have **no spare** money at all.
A slow winter cutting my hours would hurt, and **AI** has nothing to do with it.
do: Keep going and use the AI assistant a bit **more** for maths.
Ask Gus for an extra weekday **shift** in the busy season.
feel: **Flat**, in a normal-world way, while watching my balance.
S0.quote: In a normal winter I cut my shifts by a third and start eating the same pasta every night, so my worry isn't about robots
fieldNote: His **worry** is a thin winter at the shop, not AI.
He treats AI as a **patient friend** who sometimes talks nonsense.
He doesn't copy **answers**, because the exam won't allow it.

steps.text: Ask Gus for an extra weekday shift in busy season
Use the AI assistant to explain proofs I'm stuck on
Build a small emergency fund of a few hundred

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change that people are underestimating, though not apocalyptic. I'd tell my housemates it hits coding and writing first, which includes us, so we should work out what we're good at that software isn't. I'd say it with a shrug, but I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit nervous. Computer science is about the nearest course to what the card describes. If firms hire fewer juniors, the pile of applicants gets bigger and the job pile gets smaller, and I'm not a standout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my project work toward things that touch hardware, like embedded systems, because that's where my bike-shop brain is useful. I'd use AI tools more at university so I know their limits, and write down where they fail. And I'd look for an internship at a company that makes physical devices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little anxious, but oddly interested. It's like seeing a storm on the forecast and deciding which window to board up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would hardware help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the card says robots arrive more slowly in hands-on work, and someone has to design and fix things that are physical. I know what it's like to fix a real broken thing with my hands, and AI is slower at that than at writing code. That's my edge, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Gus say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say 'a bike is a bike'. He'd be right for now. But if the online ordering got smarter, he'd probably need me to set it up, and that's one more thing I could offer.

say: I'd say it's a big change people are **underestimating**, not apocalyptic.
I'd say it hits coding and writing **first**, which includes us.
think: Computer science is about the **nearest** course to what the card describes.
With fewer junior hires, I'm **not a standout** in a bigger applicant pile.
do: Move project work toward **hardware** like embedded systems.
Use AI tools more so I know their **limits**.
Look for an **internship** at a company making physical devices.
feel: **Anxious** but interested, like boarding up the right window before a storm.
S1.quote: I know what it's like to fix a real broken thing with my hands, and AI is slower at that than at writing code
fieldNote: His **bike-shop** background gives him a hardware angle he can use.
He wants to learn AI's **limits** by logging where it fails.
He admits he's **not a standout**, which makes his plan more realistic.

steps.text: Pick an embedded systems project for next term
Keep a log of where the AI assistant gets things wrong
Apply for an internship at a device maker

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, wow, that's quick, and I'd mean it. Two years is shorter than most people's phone contracts. I'd tell my housemates we should stop assuming our degrees are a ticket to anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be really worried. I've done one term, and a short time later, the thing I'm studying for is done by software that's cheaper than me. I'd feel like I'd bought a ticket to a train that left the station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay in the degree for a while, because leaving without a plan is a worse idea. I'd ask the university whether I can switch to a more hands-on course like mechatronics, and I'd go full-time at the bike shop in the holidays. I'd also get a plumbing or electrics taster day, because that's the sort of thing that outlasts the thinking jobs by a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Properly scared. I'd probably joke about it, which is how I deal with it, but my stomach would be tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your housemates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit them down in the kitchen with a pot of tea and make everyone say what their plan is. I'd make my three housemates say out loud what they'd do in two years, because a plan you've said to friends is harder to drop. It would be awkward, but useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year delay for robots help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does a bit, since it means a trade that uses hands would last longer than a coding job. But I'd still be guessing, and a trade isn't a safe place if the work moves to a robot after three years. I'd pick something that bridges the two.

say: I'd say it's **quick**: two years is shorter than most phone contracts.
I'd tell housemates our degrees are no longer a **ticket** to anything.
think: I'd feel I'd bought a ticket to a **train** that left the station.
The thing I'm studying could be done more cheaply by **software**.
do: Stay in the degree for now and ask about **mechatronics**.
Go full time at the **bike shop** in the holidays.
Try a plumbing or **electrics** taster day.
feel: Properly **scared**, joking to cope, with a tight stomach.
S2.quote: I'd make my three housemates say out loud what they'd do in two years, because a plan you've said to friends is harder to drop
fieldNote: He copes with **humour**, and the joke hides a tight stomach.
He looks for a **bridge** between thinking and hands-on work, such as mechatronics.
He wants his housemates to say their **plans** aloud.

steps.text: Ask the university about switching to mechatronics
Work full time at the bike shop in the holidays
Book a plumbing or electrics taster day
Hold off on dropping out until the next term results

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent runway, and I'd tell people to start something now. I'd say it to my housemates over dinner, probably when we're complaining about the rent. I'd also say that universities should teach what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel more settled, because five years lets me graduate and have a job for a bit. I'd be 23 when it lands, and the loan would still be there. I'd want to be in a role that looks harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with a hardware tilt, get one internship, and learn the major AI tools properly. I'd also save a little each month, so by the end I have a few months of rent. And I'd try to get a role at a firm that builds things, like machines or sensors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. It's like having a deadline for an assignment that's long, so I'll probably mess about for the first year and then panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you messing about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sticky note on my wall with the dates. I'd write 2031 on a sticky note above my desk so every time I'm tempted to waste a weekend, I remember how short five years is. It works for exams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different from the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get to choose. With two years I'd be scrambling, but with five I can study something and have a decent job in it before it changes. It's the difference between swerving and braking.

say: I'd say five years is a decent **runway**, so start now.
I'd say universities should teach what's **coming**.
think: Five years lets me **graduate** and hold a job before it lands.
I'd want a role that looks **harder** to replace.
do: Finish the degree with a **hardware** tilt and one internship.
Save a little monthly towards a few months of **rent**.
feel: **Okay**, mostly, though I'd probably mess about in year one and then panic.
S3.quote: I'd write 2031 on a sticky note above my desk so every time I'm tempted to waste a weekend, I remember how short five years is
fieldNote: Five years lets him **choose**, which he calls the difference between swerving and braking.
He expects to **procrastinate** and uses a sticky note to stop it.
His **loan** keeps the mood above uneasy.

steps.text: Choose hardware modules and finish with an embedded project
Learn the main AI coding and design tools in second year
Save a little each month towards three months of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth and last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, and it's up to us to not waste it. I'd tell my friends that it's still going to hit, so the move is to get skills that carry over. I'd probably be less loud about it than in the shorter ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine about me, because by 28 I could have a good job and savings, and I'd have time to change course twice if I needed to. The part that bugs me is that most people won't use the time, and then there'll be a rush at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do a placement, get a job in something that builds on hardware, and clear the loan in five years. I'd keep an eye on how the tools develop and learn one new thing each year. And I'd keep the bike repair as a hobby, because it's a skill that's still mine if everything else shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, honestly. A bit guilty for being relaxed while other people won't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to tell younger people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That ten years isn't forever and not to take the first job that says yes. I'd tell any first-year that ten years goes fast, so spend the first two on skills that will still matter later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if it came earlier than ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd already have savings and a skill by then, so I'd act faster, not start from nothing. That's the point of using the time.

say: I'd say ten years is **generous** and it's up to us not to waste it.
I'd tell friends to get **skills** that carry over.
think: I'd feel fine about **me**, with a good job and savings by 28.
It bugs me that most people won't use the time and will **rush** at the end.
do: Finish the degree, do a **placement** and clear the loan in five years.
Learn **one new thing** each year about the tools.
Keep **bike repair** as a hobby skill that stays mine.
feel: Pretty **relaxed**, with a bit of guilt about others who won't be.
S4.quote: I'd tell any first-year that ten years goes fast, so spend the first two on skills that will still matter later
fieldNote: Ten years makes him **relaxed**, with a plan to learn one new thing yearly.
The **rush** at the end is his main worry, for others more than for himself.
He values **bike repair** as a skill that survives any change.

steps.text: Clear the student loan within five years of starting work
Learn one new tool or skill every year
Keep fixing bikes at weekends as a hobby

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because two years means no time to choose, only to scramble. What would help is clear information from the university about which courses will still be worth it, plus help covering rent if you need to switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really, except that I'm not as laid back as I sound. I make jokes because worrying out loud makes me worse, so please don't take the jokes for not caring. I'd like a straight answer on what's coming.

headlineQuote: I make jokes because worrying out loud makes me worse, so please don't take the jokes for not caring
portrait: Ben is an **18-year-old** computer science first-year in a shared house, working at a bike repair shop.
He is centrist and steady: he uses AI now and then, and treats it as a patient friend who sometimes talks nonsense.
He has no spare money, and the shop's quiet winters hurt him more than AI does in the plain scenario.
He copes with **jokes**, but his plans are practical: hardware modules, internships, small savings.
His mood moves from uneasy to alarmed at two years, then eases to uneasy with ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries him most, because two years leaves no time to choose.
whatWouldHelp: He wants clear **information** on which courses stay worthwhile and rent help for switching.
